impassive

im-PASS-iv · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Impassive is not feeling or showing emotion.

The poker champion kept an impassive expression even when she was dealt a terrible hand, giving her opponents nothing to read.

Example

The negotiator remained impassive through hours of shouting, never once raising his voice or changing his expression.

Impassive describes a deliberately unreadable face or manner, often used to hide one's true feelings under pressure.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

detached: Detached means standing apart emotionally, as if the matter does not touch you -- a good referee stays detached from both teams. Impassive is different: an impassive person may feel a great deal but lets none of it show. Detached is about not feeling involved; impassive is about not showing.

expressionless: Expressionless describes a face that shows nothing -- blank eyes, still mouth -- whatever the cause, even simple boredom. Impassive covers the whole manner, face and voice alike, and implies control: an impassive person is deliberately keeping feeling from showing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

emotional: showing strong feelings openly

animated: full of expressive life

demonstrative: openly showing feelings

Where it sits · how firmly emotion is held in — calm → impassive → stony

calm vs. impassive: Calm is much milder than impassive: staying calm during a minor delay is easy because there is little to feel, while staying impassive means holding real emotion firmly out of sight.

stony vs. impassive: Stony goes a step beyond impassive: an impassive face gives nothing away in one hard moment, while a stony one seems carved from rock -- hour after hour, nothing at all gets through.

The pieces

prefix — im-

prefix — im-: not (Latin)

root+suffix — passive

root+suffix — passive: feeling or subject to feeling (Latin (pati))

Put it together

Put it together: im- ("not") + passive ("feeling") = not showing or being affected by feeling.

Use the root in a new word: patient

Use the root in a new word: patient: The same root, Latin pati ("to suffer or endure"), survives in the everyday word "patient" -- one who endures calmly.
